title: How to Time Your Flu Shot and Pick the Right Option This Fall
excerpt: Doctors say October is the sweet spot for most people, with enhanced shots for those 65 and older — and a new mRNA flu vaccine on the market. For travelers to India, the timing question is different.
body:
• Doctors say the ideal time to get a flu shot is September or October, before the end of October; it takes about two weeks to build full immunity.
  • Adults 65 and older should preferentially get an "enhanced" vaccine: Fluzone High-Dose, Fluad (adjuvanted) or Flublok (recombinant).
  • New for the 2026-27 season: Moderna's mFlusiva, the first FDA-approved mRNA flu vaccine, cleared for ages 50 and up and found 27% more effective than a standard shot in ages 50-64.
  • Flu, COVID and RSV vaccines can all be given in the same visit; all 2026-27 flu vaccines are trivalent.
  • India saw a sharp H1N1 surge in August; the ICMR says the Northern Hemisphere vaccine is preferable, and travelers to India should be vaccinated well before their trip.

Respiratory virus season is here, and the message from doctors is simple: October is the month to roll up your sleeve. Getting the flu shot in September or October offers the best protection through the winter peak, experts told the Associated Press this week.

"October is when I recommend getting the vaccine," said Dr. Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease specialist, via Prevention.com. "The vaccine will last further into the season if administered in October."

Why timing matters

Flu activity typically picks up in November and December, peaks from December through February, and immunity takes roughly two weeks to develop after vaccination, then wanes over about six months. That arithmetic makes October the sweet spot: vaccination covers the worst months without fading early.

Most adults should not vaccinate in July or August — especially those 65 and older or in early pregnancy — because protection could fade before the season ends. Young children needing two doses (ages 6 months to 8 years, never vaccinated) are the exception: they should start as soon as vaccine is available so the second dose lands by the end of October.

"Vaccination isn't a guarantee that we're going to prevent illness. But just like the seat belt in your car, it decreases risk of the worst outcomes."

— Dr. Ryan Stanton, American College of Emergency Physicians

Missed the October window? It's not an expiration date: the CDC says vaccination should continue through the season while flu is circulating. Matthew S. Miller, PhD, of McMaster University, told Medscape that delaying risks infection before immunity can develop.

Which shot to pick

All 2026-27 flu vaccines are trivalent, protecting against two influenza A strains and one B/Victoria-lineage virus. For adults 65 and older, the CDC preferentially recommends one of three "enhanced" vaccines — Fluzone High-Dose, Fluad (adjuvanted) or Flublok (recombinant). "But do not delay your vaccination if that one's not available," Dr. Sarah Nosal of the American Academy of Family Physicians told the AP.

The new option this season is Moderna's mFlusiva, the first mRNA flu vaccine approved by the FDA (August 2026), for adults 50 and older. One study found it 27% more effective against symptomatic illness in ages 50-64 than a standard shot; side effects were somewhat more common, and some insurers may not yet cover it.

For the needle-averse, the FluMist nasal spray covers ages 2 to 49 who are not pregnant and have no underlying conditions. People with egg allergies can receive any age-appropriate flu vaccine; pregnant people can get standard shots in any trimester, but not the nasal spray.

One visit, three vaccines

Flu, COVID and RSV vaccines can all be given in the same visit — in different arms — with side effects similar to getting them separately. The FDA has approved 2026-27 COVID shots primarily for higher-risk groups; RSV is a one-time dose for ages 75 and up and for 50-74 at increased risk, plus pregnant women between 32 and 36 weeks.

The India angle

For the diaspora, the flu question isn't just an American one. India saw a sharp H1N1 surge in August: a LocalCircles survey found 54% of 32,000+ households reported at least one member with flu-like symptoms, and WHO surveillance for early September found influenza positivity of 22% across the South-East Asia region, with A(H1N1)pdm09 accounting for 75% of India's positive samples. India's ICMR says the Northern Hemisphere vaccine is preferable but the Southern Hemisphere formulation is also effective — and travelers to India should vaccinate well before the trip, since India's flu season peaks with the monsoon months, not the Western winter.

Flu-vaccine demand in India tripled in August versus a year earlier, causing supply constraints in some cities.

Do they work?

Last season, the flu vaccine reduced older-adult hospitalizations by 31%, per the Vaccine Integrity Project at the University of Minnesota. Flu causes hundreds of thousands of hospitalizations and tens of thousands of US deaths each year — and the last two seasons brought unusually high child deaths, the vast majority in unvaccinated children, the AP notes.
